text: System Design Methodology Framework Allocate specific time slots: 5m for requirements, 20m for high-level design, 15m for deep dive, and 5m for wrapping up. - Define requirements and use cases - functional requirements first, and non-functional requirements if obvious - a good framing could be: "users should be able to..." - Start with the simplest happy path, then deep dive later - add more non-functional requirements if you think about them later - consistency Vs availability - On that example, clarify the priority in the context. - For example with Ticketmaster, consistency is way more important, but for rate limiters, availability is more important - read vs write ratio - access pattern (hot vs cold) - narrow down scope and verify with interviewer - you can suggest cutting down scope too - List core entities - Quickly list the data and its type - Don't write proper models yet until fleshed out further or prompted - Find rough load parameters to get an idea of the scale - Do maths estimations only if it servers a purpose. Do it only if it changes your design - Ie if the data is big enough to force a database sharing or if one database is enough. - Things like - How many users - Amount of data - Practicing quick maths will help here - Layout simple high level components, avoid early optimisation - Deep dive - Mention example technology, ideally more in the deep dive section - mention if used to or not used to a certain technology sometimes - propose multiple solutions, and discuss trade-offs with data - Show understanding between complexity and scale. - match system design to actual scale (ie, only bring sharding if necessary) - Wrap Up - Run through a use case once components are layed out, test your own setup - Question to ask at the end: did all the agreed requirements and non functional requirements pass with the design and the use cases run-through? - If not and time is up, probably highlight what you'd look into next - Think about what could go wrong, and list some obvious edge cases you can think of - What if all users want the same thing as a spike - Introduce new dimension or directions it could go at the end - Consider challenging your own design with different axes - Scalability - Maintainability Things to keep in mind - lead the conversation but keep it a conversation: avoid asking them for insight if you're stuck, that might be interpreted as you're not senior enough - Take notes, make assumptions, lay them out and verify them sometimes - List what's involved, share your knowledge of the existing thing and ask if anything needs to be corrected - Ask where to focus on or deep dive once you have a few options, with a possibility to start with your preference - Try to be upfront on decision making - SQL vs NoSQL is not that interesting of a chat, especially as a senior - What's more interesting is whether you need consistency and ACID (both can do that well these days), the use cases (ie search or caching) and the context - Get familiar with tools like excalidraw - Don't just write low latency, specify a number if you do - Expectations - Seniors are expected to be more proactive with issues and limitations like a single refis is not enough - Staff could explain stories on how they had to deal with similar scenarios, what they did and learned - Don't use memorised answers - Focus on what I know rather than theory books - Be clear on what you don't know and what you have experience with - text: What you're really assessing for - Can they do the job? - Not necessarily right, now but you need to know that they can learn how to do it. - Unless you have constraints that they need to be performant straight away. - Will they get better at doing the job? This is especially relevant for juniors Traits to look for From Blog - You suck at technical interviews: - Relevant experience is a plus but not a requirement - Somebody who is constantly improving is a requirement - Smart and Gets Things Done™ - Somebody who can intelligently discuss technology - Somebody who knows what they don't know - This is a conversation, not an interrogation - The final question: do I want to work with this person? What not to hire From Blog - You suck at technical interviews: Don't hire for what they already know Don't hire for what they can remember in an interview room Note on diversity You don't want to just hire people like you, which "would I work with this person" can sometimes seem like it's mainly answering. From Blog - You suck at technical interviews: This makes it a personality test, and that makes it very, very dangerous territory. Personality is subjective, and that means you are inviting bias into the equation. Personal bias, implicit bias, unconscious bias. You are NOT hiring for "team fit" I have never heard a definition of "team fit" that didn't end up sounding like "let our bias run free". Phrases like "looks like they belong here" are terrifying - The distinction is subtle, but important: somebody who is good for your team is not necessarily somebody you want to be friends with. It's tempting to look for both, but it's the wrong metric for the success of your company and is ultimately unsustainable - Homogeneity is disastrous - Instead of hiring for "best for the job" you have accidentally hired for "looks like me". - The important thing to remember is that hiring a bad person is more expensive and wastes more time than waiting for a good person.

headings: When to use caching Cache eviction policies Use cases Hot search terms Reduce load on main db Ways to cache In-memory caching Edge cases Database requests burst when TTLs expire Hot caches Resource
text: Cache trade off speed vs freshness Caching patterns When to use caching From Youtube - Hello Interview – Caching in System Design Interviews w Meta Staff Engineer: - read heavy workload (millions) - expensive queries (like catalog post processing) - when database CPU is high, reduce load - latency (when you need it to be faster ) Cache eviction policies From Google: Least Frequently Used (LFU) and Least Recently Used (LRU) are two core cache eviction policies used to clear space when a cache is full, but they decide what to delete using different signals. - LRU (Least Recently Used): Evicts the item that has not been touched for the longest amount of time . It measures recency. - LFU (Least Frequently Used): Evicts the item that has the lowest total number of accesses . It measures frequency Use cases Hot search terms You can also use the CDN as a cache for api results. Short term. Ok if only a few Consider how often it changes, how long it's cached. If you cache it, then you can't personalise it. Same with html pages, you can cache a home page only if it's the same for everyone (at least for a certain region per CDN). Number of urls could become expensive if lots of query params Reduce load on main db From Youtube - Hello Interview – Caching in System Design Interviews w Meta Staff Engineer: Reading from memory is 10k times faster than reading from disk. For read heavy systems, you can reduce load on db by introducing a key value cache in front. Especially for data that doesn't change often, then you don't have to invalidate cache often That allows keeping just one postgres for example. But be wary of single points of failure if the cache dies for example, be ready to have more DBs for reads anyway Ways to cache In-memory caching In-memory caching (or memoization) works in some scenarios, for example for caching all data in a table if the table is quite small (like a small table of retailers). Edge cases Database requests burst when TTLs expire If you cache on service start and all servers start at the same time, it'll burst the db in requests. Or if all TTLs expire at the same time. To remediate, you can use "cache warming" where you query the db before the cache expires. Hot caches If a key is requested a lot, you can: - load balance it across nodes - keep an in-memory cache for hot keys in apps/clients - be more granular in the cache key - request coalescing (if multiple requests are the same, trigger only one and return the result for all clients) Resource Youtube - Hello Interview – Caching in System Design Interviews w Meta Staff Engineer Youtube - Maddy Zhang – 900+ hours of Learning System Design in 9 Minutes

title: Consistency
text: Weak consistency After a write, reads may or may not see it. A best effort approach is taken. This approach is seen in systems such as memcached. Weak consistency works well in real time use cases such as VoIP, video chat, and realtime multiplayer games. For example, if you are on a phone call and lose reception for a few seconds, when you regain connection you do not hear what was spoken during connection loss. Eventual consistency After a write, reads will eventually see it (typically within milliseconds). Data is replicated asynchronously. This approach is seen in systems such as DNS and email. Eventual consistency works well in highly available systems. Strong consistency After a write, reads will see it. Data is replicated synchronously. This approach is seen in file systems and RDBMSes. Strong consistency works well in systems that need transactions.

title: Availability
text: Availability patterns There are two main patterns to support high availability: fail-over and replication. Fail-over Active-passive With active-passive fail-over, heartbeats are sent between the active and the passive server on standby. If the heartbeat is interrupted, the passive server takes over the active's IP address and resumes service. The length of downtime is determined by whether the passive server is already running in 'hot' standy or whether it needs to start up from 'cold' standby. Only the active server handles traffic. Active-passive failover can also be referred to as master-slave failover. Active-active In active-active, both servers are managing traffic, spreading the load between them. If the servers are public-facing, the DNS would need to know about the public IPs of both servers. If the servers are internal-facing, application logic would need to know about both servers. Active-active failover can also be referred to as master-master failover. Disadvantage(s): failover Fail-over adds more hardware and additional complexity. There is a potential for loss of data if the active system fails before any newly written data can be replicated to the passive. Replication Master-slave replication The master serves reads and writes, replicating writes to one or more slaves, which serve only reads. Slaves can also replicate to additional slaves in a tree-like fashion. If the master goes offline, the system can continue to operate in read-only mode until a slave is promoted to a master or a new master is provisioned. Source: Scalability, availability, stability, patterns Disadvantage(s): master-slave replication Additional logic is needed to promote a slave to a master. See Disadvantage(s): replication for points related to both master-slave and master-master. Master-master replication Both masters serve reads and writes and coordinate with each other on writes. If either master goes down, the system can continue to operate with both reads and writes. Source: Scalability, availability, stability, patterns Disadvantage(s): master-master replication You'll need a load balancer or you'll need to make changes to your application logic to determine where to write. Most master-master systems are either loosely consistent (violating ACID) or have increased write latency due to synchronization. Conflict resolution comes more into play as more write nodes are added and as latency increases. See Disadvantage(s): replication for points related to both master-slave and master-master. Disadvantage(s): replication There is a potential for loss of data if the master fails before any newly written data can be replicated to other nodes. Writes are replayed to the read replicas. If there are a lot of writes, the read replicas can get bogged down with replaying writes and can't do as many reads. The more read slaves, the more you have to replicate, which leads to greater replication lag. On some systems, writing to the master can spawn multiple threads to write in parallel, whereas read replicas only support writing sequentially with a single thread. Replication adds more hardware and additional complexity. Source(s) and further reading: replication Scalability, availability, stability, patterns Multi-master replication

title: Message queues
headings: When to use system queues Difference between message queue and stream at least once vs at most once vs exactly once at least once at most once exactly once How to ensure that messages are consumed by only 1 consumer at a time Ordering Partitioning How to deal with queues growing Kafka vs SQS vs Kinesis Resource
text: When to use system queues - operations too long for a live server, get feedback to users quickly - reduce load on a live server - when you want the ability to scale differently for different tasks (ie retrievers need less memory than collectors in dogs) - reliability: keep messages to be processed in queue until workers are healthy again Difference between message queue and stream Kafka can be used as a queue, but main use case alongside Kinesis is streaming. For Kafka: The key difference between the two lies in the consumption pattern. When used as a message queue, each message is processed by one consumer in a group and then effectively "consumed" (though Kafka still retains it based on retention policy). When used as a stream, consumers continuously process messages as they arrive in real-time, and the same data can be read by multiple independent consumer groups or replayed from any point in the log. at least once vs at most once vs exactly once Message queues can be at least once, at most once or exactly once (hard). at least once Default approach if you're ok with messages sometimes being processed more than once. Messages need to be idempotent for this to work (no side effect if you process it twice). - set balance + 1: not idempotent as it relies on the previous state - set balance to 54: idempotent as it can be processed multiple times and achieve the same outcome at most once if a message cannot be processed more than once, then consumers can ack as soon as they get the message. there is no guarantee however that it will succeed at processing the message. you have to be ok with messages being lost sometimes exactly once hard. don't promise you can do that unless you can explain how it works, apparently kafka has some way to get close to that How to ensure that messages are consumed by only 1 consumer at a time SQS makes messages invisible after a consumer acquires it. When it acknowledges it, it will delete it. If it doesn't after a certain time, it will become available for consumption again. This is essentially how "at least once" works. Kafka makes partitions so that messages will only ever be consumed by a certain consumer. 1 partition 1 consumer. Ordering Ordering can be guaranteed within a partition, make sure you put messages that need to be processed in order in the same partition. SQS offers different options of ordering. Partitioning Careful when you create your partition key that you're not creating hot partitions (same concept as Database Sharding). How to deal with queues growing Add more consumers. Add back pressure (make producers produce less). Kafka vs SQS vs Kinesis Kafka is pub/sub (multiple subscribers). SQS is queue (1 consumer for 1 queue). SNS allows publishing messages and creating multiple unique queues out of it (fannout pattern). SQS remembers messages for up to 4 days. SQS has limited size per message (256kb). Kinesis is more for real time streaming. Continuous stream, multiple subscribers. Kinesis is basically Kafka but using more the AWS stuff. title: Forward proxy vs Reverse proxy vs API Gateway
text: Forward proxy: next to the client before reaching internet Reverse proxy: server side to go to the right server API gateway: reverse proxy that does more than routing. it handles auth, rate limiting and other things before going to the right API A forward proxy sits next to the client. Your laptop sends a request, the proxy forwards it out, and the destination never sees your real IP. Corporate networks use this to enforce policy, block sites, and cache traffic. A reverse proxy sits next to the server. The client has no idea how many machines are behind it. The proxy decides who handles the request, terminates TLS, and keeps your backend off the public internet. NGINX and HAProxy are commonly used here, typically paired with a load balancer in front. An API gateway is a reverse proxy that does more than route traffic. It also handles auth, rate limits, API keys, versioning, and request shaping. Without it, each microservice has to implement its own version of validation, throttling logic, and request logging. A forward proxy represents the client, a reverse proxy represents the server, and an API gateway is what you add when ten services need the same authentication and rate limiting rules applied consistently. In most real systems, all three are running at different layers. The forward proxy filters outbound traffic, the reverse proxy fronts the application servers, and the API gateway sits in front of your APIs to enforce policies before requests reach them.

title: Reverse proxy vs API gateway vs load balancer
text: Reverse proxy An API gateway is a specialized type of reverse proxy From Google: While a load balancer , a reverse proxy , and an API gateway look similar because they all sit between clients and backend services, they serve entirely different purposes. The easiest way to differentiate them is by their core focus: a load balancer focuses on scale , a reverse proxy focuses on security and optimization , and an API gateway focuses on application logic and API management . Direct Comparison Feature Reverse Proxy Load Balancer API Gateway --- --- --- --- Primary Goal Protects, caches, and isolates backend web servers. Distributes traffic to prevent server overload. Manages, secures, and routes individual API endpoints. Traffic Focus General web traffic (HTTP/HTTPS, static files). Network layers (TCP/UDP) or application layers (HTTP). Application APIs (REST, GraphQL, gRPC). Typical Tools NGINX, Apache, HAProxy AWS ALB, F5 BIG-IP, HAProxy Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway --- 1. Reverse Proxy (The Shield & Booster) A reverse proxy sits in front of a web server to shield its identity, optimize performance, and handle incoming requests. It acts as an intermediary so clients never talk directly to your actual application servers. - Main Job: Privacy, security, and offloading repetitive tasks. - Key Capabilities: - SSL/TLS Termination: It handles the heavy encryption/decryption work so backend servers don't have to. - Caching: It stores copies of popular static content (like images or CSS) and serves them instantly without hitting your backend. - Anonymity: It hides the IP addresses and structures of your internal infrastructure from the public internet. 2. API Gateway (The Smart Concierge) An API gateway is a specialized type of reverse proxy designed specifically for modern microservices architectures. It doesn't just pass requests along; it inspects, translates, and manipulates them based on application rules. - Main Job: Orchestrating API requests and enforcing business logic at the edge. - Key Capabilities: - Request Routing / Composition: It can take a single request from a mobile app, fetch data from three separate backend microservices (e.g., Users, Inventory, and Shipping), combine the data, and send back one clean response. - Authentication & Authorization: It checks if a user's API token is valid before letting the request reach any microservices. - Rate Limiting & Throttling: It blocks users who try to spam or abuse specific endpoints (e.g., limiting a user to 60 requests per minute). - Protocol Translation: It can convert an incoming REST request into an internal gRPC request. --- How They Work Together In a large production environment, you will often see all three layered together to form a robust architecture: 1. A Load Balancer sits at the very front to split incoming traffic across multiple instances. 2. The traffic hits a Reverse Proxy to strip away SSL encryption and handle basic caching. 3. The request is passed to the API Gateway , which authorizes the user's API token and routes them to the correct backend microservice.

title: Database Sharding
headings: When to use sharding Trade offs Sharding methods Hashing How to choose a shard key What not to do Directory based sharding Issues with sharding Cross-shards requests Remediation Consistency Resource
text: When to use sharding - Write-heavy: Too much data for 1 instance (storage or write per second) - Read-heavy: when read replicas or caching are not enough Trade offs - Global queries will be slower - Complexity to operate and keep data consistent Sharding methods Hashing Needs to be consistent (consistent hashing ). How to choose a shard key - high cardinality (lots of values to spread) - even distribution so that every shard has the same amount of data - when you query, you need only one shard To avoid hot spots, perhaps you can shard a bit more granular, ie not just bye user id but by user id + post creation date What not to do Boolean is very low cardinality Sharding by creation date where most people query the most recent year makes one shard hot, not evenly distributed Range based sharding, like by user id might make hot shards, all users in one shard depending on how many Directory based sharding You can do directory based sharding where you stored somewhere in which shard the data is. Allows flexibility you can easily change in which shard something is ik case it's really hot, but it adds lots of latency as you need to look it up every time. Adds a single point of failure too. You can do something hybrid where you manually store for hot keys in which shard they are stored, and use the normal hashing method for the rest. Issues with sharding Cross-shards requests Some queries might need data across shards, and this could become really slow. Remediation You can cache expensive cross shard queries. This is where de normalisation could have a use case, let the related data live in the same shard but multiple writes Consistency From Youtube - Hello Interview – Distributed Transactions Explained 2 Phase Commit vs Saga Pattern: Another way to see sharding would be going down the microservice route, with dedicated databases. headings: Data limits for one instance How much data is too much for 1 instance?
text: Data limits for one instance - read: 20k queries per second - write: 10k writes per second How much data is too much for 1 instance? From google: A single PostgreSQL database can technically store up to 32 TB per table, but "too much" data usually starts at 100 GB to 1 TB for practical application performance on standard hardware. - Under 100 GB: Fast and easy. Most queries run instantly if you use basic indexes. Routine maintenance tasks like VACUUM take only seconds. - 100 GB to 1 TB: The transition zone. Performance depends heavily on your RAM. If your active working data fits inside your server's memory, everything stays fast. If queries must constantly read from the disk, things slow down. - 1 TB to 10+ TB: Too large for a single unoptimized table. Maintenance tasks like backups, full table scans, and index rebuilds take hours and can lock resources or saturate your CPU. How to Scale Past the Limit - Partitioning: Split large tables by date or region so Postgres only searches the relevant slice of data. - Improve Hardware: Upgrade to faster NVMe storage and add more RAM so the kernel can cache more data. - Sharding: Split data across multiple independent PostgreSQL clusters if a single machine's CPU and I/O limits are fully maxed out.

title: Caching patterns
headings: Cache aside vs Read through Write through vs Write back
text: Cache aside vs Read through - Cache aside: app checks cache and fetches from DB on miss then updates cache - Read through: app checks cache, the cache will automatically fetch from the DB if missing The difference between the 2 above, is what is fetching from the DB on cache miss. Either the app or the cache system itself, but the principle is the same. Benefit of readthrough is that the app code only needs to fetch from the cache and the cache logic manages what happens on miss. If you need to invalidate the cache, you can manually remove the key. If consistency matters, you can invalidate on DB write so that the next read triggers a refresh from DB. Write through vs Write back - Write through: app writes to the cache and then to the DB - Write behind (or back): app writes to the cache and queues an update to the DB for later The main difference is the data consistency. Write behind is eventually consistent, but faster. From Google: Strategy How it Works Read Speed Write Speed Data Consistency Best Used For --- --- --- --- --- --- Cache-Aside The application manually checks the cache, fetches from the database on a miss, and updates the cache. Fast (on hit) Fast Eventual (requires app manual eviction) General purpose, read-heavy workloads with unpredictable query patterns Read-Through The application asks the cache for data, and the cache automatically pulls it from the database if missing. Fast (on hit) Normal Eventual (managed by cache provider) Read-heavy workloads where you want to keep cache logic out of the app code Write-Through The application writes data to the cache, and the cache immediately saves it to the database before finishing. Fast Slow Strong (cache and DB update together) Applications that cannot tolerate stale data (e.g., banking ledger balances) Write-Behind The application writes data to the cache, which acknowledges it instantly and saves to the database later in batches. Fast Fastest Eventual (DB updates lag behind cache) Write-heavy workloads with high bursts (e.g., IoT data streams, real-time gaming scores) --- Key Takeaways & Trade-offs - Application vs. Cache Responsibility: Cache-Aside requires you to write the fallback logic inside your application code. Read-Through abstracts this away, moving the database fetching responsibility entirely to the caching infrastructure. - The Write Speed vs. Data Safety Dilemma: Write-Through guarantees strong consistency and zero data loss, but it penalizes application write performance with dual network round-trips. Write-Behind provides maximum speed by writing to memory first, but you risk losing data if the cache crashes before syncing to the database. - Memory Optimization: Patterns like Cache-Aside and Read-Through only load data on demand, keeping memory costs low. Write-intensive patterns can cause cache churn by filling memory with data that may never be read again.

title: Engineering manager core skills
headings: Self-assessing on these skills
text: From Blog - Good engineering management is a fad: I think there are eight foundational engineering management skills, which I want to personally group into two clusters: core skills that are essential to operate in all roles (including entry-level management roles), and growth skills whose presence–or absence–determines how far you can go in your career. - The core skills are: - - Execution : lead team to deliver expected tangible and intangible work. Fundamentally, management is about getting things done, and you’ll neither get an opportunity to begin managing, nor stay long as a manager, if your teams don’t execute. Examples : ship projects, manage on-call rotation, sprint planning, manage incidents - - Team : shape the team and the environment such that they succeed. This is not working for the team, nor is it working for your leadership, it is finding the balance between the two that works for both. Examples : hiring, coaching, performance management, advocate with your management - - Ownership : navigate reality to make consistent progress, even when reality is difficult Finding a way to get things done, rather than finding a way that it’s not getting done is someone else’s fault. Examples : doing hard things, showing up when it’s uncomfortable, being accountable despite systemic issues - - Alignment : build shared understanding across leadership, stakeholders, your team, and the problem space. Finding a realistic plan that meets the moment, without surprising or being surprised by those around you. Examples : document and share top problems, and updates during crises - The growth skills are: - - Taste : exercise discerning judgment about what “good” looks like—technically, in business terms, and in process/strategy. Taste is a broad church, and my experience is that broad taste is a somewhat universal criterion for truly senior roles. In some ways, taste is a prerequisite to Amazon’s Are Right, A Lot. Examples : refine proposed product concept, avoid high-risk rewrite, find usability issues in team’s work - - Clarity : your team, stakeholders, and leadership know what you’re doing and why, and agree that it makes sense. In particular, they understand how you are overcoming your biggest problems. title: Shipping projects
headings: What is shipping, really The role of the tech lead when shipping Competence and confidence Gaining trust Communication
text: What is shipping, really Shipping is a social construct within a company. Concretely, that means that a project is shipped when the important people at your company believe it is shipped. It's not when it's deployed, it's when it's acknowledged by leadership and socially celebrated. If you deploy your system, but your manager or VP or CEO is very unhappy with it, you did not ship . (Maybe you shipped something, but you didn’t ship the actual project.) If you ship something users hate and makes no money, but your leadership team is happy, you still shipped . The role of the tech lead when shipping First, you have to get clear on what the company is looking to get out of the project . Shipping should be the priority of someone, usually the tech lead. it’s really important that one person on the project has an end-to-end understanding of the whole thing: how it hangs together technically, and what product or business purpose it serves For the teams that don't have a tech lead: projects live and die based on whether an engineer steps up into this role of their own accord. Competence and confidence you have the most end-to-end context on the project, which means you should be the least scared of scary changes . Gaining trust they will be trusting you for estimates, to answer technical questions, and to anticipate technical problems. Maintaining that trust should be your top priority . If they don’t have faith in your ability to do the job and to keep them informed, you will not ship. your manager will be much happier going to their manager about it if they can say something like “our options are to delay four days, or ship tomorrow by sacrificing X” — even if sacrificing X is a non-starter. Communication Communicate professionally and concisely, and don’t make them chase you for updates: post a daily or weekly thread somewhere It is much, much more important to do these things than for the project to ship with zero bugs on the exact deadline. - If a project has to be delayed for technical reasons, in my experience you will not suffer consequences so long as you communicate it clearly, confidently (and ideally with some warning).

The Zero Interest Rate Policy (ZIRP) is when a central bank (such as the U.S. Federal Reserve or the Bank of Japan) keeps its main interest rate at or very close to 0% to encourage borrowing and spending. Think of it like this Imagine money is a product that banks sell. - Normal times: Borrowing money costs, say, 5%. - ZIRP: Borrowing money costs almost nothing (0–0.5%). When borrowing is cheap: - People buy more houses and cars. - Businesses borrow to expand. - Investors look for higher returns because bank savings pay almost nothing. --- Why do governments do this? Usually during or after a recession. The goal is to: - Encourage companies to invest. - Encourage consumers to spend. - Increase hiring. - Prevent the economy from shrinking further. --- Why was this great for tech companies? Tech companies often need lots of money before they become profitable. For example: A startup wants to build an AI product. - Revenue: £0 - Expenses: £10 million/year It needs investors to keep funding it. When interest rates rise, future money is "discounted" more heavily, so those distant profits are worth less today. Central banks raised interest rates to fight inflation. Effects: - Borrowing became more expensive. - Investors became more cautious. - Startup funding declined. - Many tech companies reduced hiring or laid off staff. - Company valuations fell, particularly for businesses that were expected to generate profits far in the future.

title: AI multi agent patterns
text: From Blog - 🧱 Your Multi-Agent Architecture Is a 2016 Microservices Diagram With the Boxes Renamed: - Router. A cheap classifier reads the request and forwards it to exactly one specialist, one hop with no synthesis step. - - Use for: support triage, intent routing in a product assistant, any case where the categories are known and the work per category is self-contained - - Router model: your cheapest one, a fine-tuned classifier, or a regex if the categories are clean enough - - Common mistake: letting the router “help” by adding context. It should classify and get out of the way - Orchestrator-worker. One capable model decomposes the task, dispatches subtasks to workers, and synthesizes the results. Workers are stateless, parallel, and can run on a different model than the orchestrator. - This is where the cost story lives: - - Orchestrator-tier and worker-tier models from the same vendor sit 5x to 15x apart on per-token price - - In a decomposed task, most tokens are worker tokens - - The number circulating in vendor write-ups this year is a 40 to 60 percent cost reduction versus running everything on the frontier model. Those write-ups are selling something, but the mechanism is sound - - Anthropic’s public data point: an Opus lead with Sonnet subagents beat single-agent Opus by 90.2 percent on their research eval. The same post reports multi-agent runs burn ~15x the tokens of a chat interaction, which is the other half of that ledger - Two rules for making it pay: - - Workers get a schema, an example, and a budget. Nothing else - - The orchestrator sees results, never raw worker transcripts, or your context bill grows with every worker you add - Supervisor. A loop rather than a fan-out. One model holds the plan, calls an agent, reads the result, revises the plan, calls the next one. - - Sequential and stateful. The supervisor’s context accumulates every result - - Use for: long-horizon tasks where step N depends on step N-1 (coding agents, migration tooling, multi-stage pipelines) - - Wrong for: anything parallelizable. title: System Design Solutions: When to use Cassandra and when not to
text: - Cassandra works really well if you want to write and store a large amount of data in a distributed system, don’t care much about ACID with good performance - people joke that it’s more difficult to run it as a single node system than as a distributed one. Most traditional databases rely on master nodes and slave nodes. text: - - Router. It should classify and get out of the way - Orchestrator-worker. One capable model decomposes the task, dispatches subtasks to workers, and synthesizes the results. Workers are stateless, parallel, and can run on a different model than the orchestrator. - This is where the cost story lives: - - Orchestrator-tier and worker-tier models from the same vendor sit 5x to 15x apart on per-token price - - In a decomposed task, most tokens are worker tokens - - The number circulating in vendor write-ups this year is a 40 to 60 percent cost reduction versus running everything on the frontier model. Nothing else - - The orchestrator sees results, never raw worker transcripts, or your context bill grows with every worker you add - Supervisor. A loop rather than a fan-out. One model holds the plan, calls an agent, reads the result, revises the plan, calls the next one. - - Sequential and stateful. The supervisor’s context accumulates every result - - Use for: long-horizon tasks where step N depends on step N-1 (coding agents, migration tooling, multi-stage pipelines) - - Wrong for: anything parallelizable. title: Work on what matters.
text: - increasingly senior roles require that you accomplish more and more, and do it in less and less time - at some point you’re going to run out of things that are both high-impact and easy. Many companies conflate high-visibility and high-impact so strongly that they can’t distinguish between preening and impact, which is why it’s not uncommon to see some companies’ senior-most engineers spend the majority of their time doing work of dubious value but that is frequently recognized in company meetings. - Sometimes you’ll find work that’s worthy of attention, but which an organization is incapable of paying attention to, usually because its leadership doesn’t value that work. In some companies this is developer tooling work, in others it’s inclusion work, and in most companies it’s glue work. - Teaching a company to value something it doesn’t care about is considerably the hardest sort of work you can do, and it often fails, so you should do as little of it as you can, but no less. As a senior leader, you have an ethical obligation that goes beyond maximizing your company-perceived impact, but it’s important to recognize what you’re up against and time your efforts accordingly. - much more important is the sort of work that simply won’t happen if you don’t do it. - This work is an intersection of what you’re exceptionally good at and what you genuinely care about. - If you spend your career snacking, preening or chasing ghosts, it’s possible but relatively unlikely that what you’ve done before will be valued at companies you interview with. Instead, the only viable long-term bet on your career is to do work that matters, work that develops you, and to steer towards companies that value genuine expertise. In summary, sustaining a successful career as time becomes scarcer requires prioritizing high-leverage work that only you can do—such as editing critical projects or fostering team growth—while actively resisting the traps of \\"snacking\\" on easy tasks, \\"preening\\" for false visibility, and \\"chasing ghosts\\" by misapplying past experiences. - Avoid low-value patterns: Resist \\"snacking\\" (low-impact/easy work), \\"preening\\" (high-visibility/low-impact work), and \\"chasing ghosts\\" (misguided shifts based on ego or irrelevant past contexts). - Prioritize with context: Swarm existential risks immediately; for non-existential issues, seek areas with room to grow where you can make rapid progress rather than competing in overcrowded priorities. - Leverage seniority through editing and finishing: Use your relationships and experience to make small changes that shift outcomes significantly, and coach others to finish projects, turning risk into leverage. - Invest in team growth: Dedicate time to mentoring and onboarding; this is underinvested yet highly leveraged work that defines a lasting legacy beyond individual output. - Pursue unique impact: Focus on work at the intersection of your exceptional skills and genuine care that simply won't happen if you don't do it, ensuring long-term career value. We all have a finite amount of time to live, and within that mortal countdown we devote some fraction towards our work.
